passage: It started with a burnt dosa. My mother said, "You never watch the stove," and something in me snapped. I told her I was sick of the comments on my flat, my job, my friends, and the way she told Himani, my wife, what to buy. Then I said she had ruined our first year of marriage. My father stood up. Words came out that I cannot take back. The thing I had meant to ask, that they call before visiting, never got said. By evening nobody was speaking, and the only thing anyone remembered was the last sentence I shouted. I have thought about it many times: I had a fair request, and I buried it under years of complaints. - Vikram

qa.q: What did the quarrel start with?
qa.a: It started with a burnt dosa.

qa.q: What was Vikram feeling underneath the outburst?
qa.a: Vikram was feeling built-up frustration from years of comments, which came out all at once.
Vikram could apologise for the shouting and later ask calmly, on its own, for the parents to call before visiting.

qa.q: How might Vikram's mother have felt when the request got lost?
qa.a: Vikram's mother may have felt hurt and confused, since the only thing that came through was the anger.

grounding: After a small quarrel Vikram blurts out a long-held complaint about the parents' interference, and the real request gets lost.

passage:
Family session notes, 18 October.
Chetan came with both parents to talk about his wish to move into his own flat near work. The first twenty minutes were calm. Then his mother mentioned, lightly, that he had left his wet towel on the bed again. Chetan's voice rose: "This is exactly it. You check my phone bill, you call my office, you chose my college, you're still choosing my life!" His father said, "After everything we've done?" His mother began to cry.
The actual request, the flat, did not come up again in the session. When I asked Chetan afterwards what he had come to ask for, he said quietly, "Just the flat. I wasn't even going to bring up the rest."
We have agreed on a second session in which Chetan will open with the request itself, written down, and the older complaints will be raised separately.
— Zainab

qa.q: What did Chetan's mother mention that set things off?
qa.a: That he had left his wet towel on the bed again.

qa.q: What was Chetan feeling when his voice rose?
qa.a: He felt long-held frustration and resentment boiling over, set off by a small comment.

qa.q: What could Chetan do in the second session?
qa.a: Open with the request for the flat, written down, and raise the older complaints separately and calmly.

qa.q: How did Chetan's parents experience the outburst?
qa.a: His father felt unappreciated, asking "After everything we've done?", and his mother was hurt enough to cry.

grounding: It shows a young man blurting out long-held complaints about his parents' interference after a small remark, so hurtful words fly and his real request is lost.

passage:
Chetan's diary, Sunday night.
It started with the curtains. Mummy said the new ones in my room were too dark. That's all. And I just exploded: about her ringing Nirmala Didi to check on me, about Papa messaging my boss, about them choosing which relatives come to the engagement. Twenty years of it came out in five minutes. Papa called me ungrateful. I said something about them never letting me breathe. Mummy walked out of the room.
The thing I actually wanted to ask was simple: can the engagement be small, family only? I never got to it. Now it's buried under everything else.
Nirmala Didi called at ten and said, "You had one point, and you made it into a war." Didi's right. Tomorrow I'll apologise for the curtains fight and ask about the engagement separately, calmly.

qa.q: What did Mummy say about the curtains?
qa.a: That the new ones were too dark.

qa.q: How does Chetan feel about the real request being lost?
qa.a: Chetan feels regretful and frustrated that the simple request for a small engagement got buried under the outburst.

qa.q: What is a better way for Chetan to raise the engagement?
qa.a: Apologise for the fight first, then ask about the small engagement on its own, at a calm moment.

qa.q: How does Nirmala Didi see the fight?
qa.a: Nirmala Didi sees that Chetan had one point and turned it into a war, and says so plainly.

grounding: It shows a small quarrel turning into an angry outburst about parents' interference, so hurtful words are exchanged and the real request is lost.
